analytic.title: Design Space Exploration of HEVC RCL Mapped onto NoC-Based Embedded Platforms

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Nowadays, several applications running into embedded systems have to meet hard/soft real-time constraints. Generally, multimedia applications, like the modern High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) standard, present soft timing constraints. However, specific scenarios like robotic surgeries and coupling of satellites require hard real-time constraints, becoming a huge challenge. Although the implementation of such applications (or part of them) in Networks-on-Chip (NoC) and the use of hardware acceleration arise as alternatives to fulfill timing constraints, a design space exploration evaluating the NoC mapping and the hardware acceleration usage, with a schedulability analysis, is mandatory. In this work we perform a design space exploration of HEVC Residual Coding Loop (RCL) mapped onto a NoC-based embedded platform, combining traditional CPUs and hardware accelerators as processing elements (PEs). We considered the encoding of a single frame, with two different resolutions: 1920x1080 and 3840x2160 pixels, when running at CPUs and hardware accelerators, respectively. A set of analysis exploring the combination of different NoC configurations and task mapping strategies were performed, with the development of a search algorithm called SNFT (Schedulability breakdown NoC Frequency Tracking algorithm), as a way to find the minimum NoC frequency for each configuration which becomes the system fully schedulable, showing for the typical and upper-bound workload cases scenarios when the application is schedulable and meets the real-time constraints.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Currently, mainly due to the fast popularization of handheld devices, the digital videos are present in our daily lives. According to [1], approximately 70% of all video visualizations on internet happen at these devices. The growth on the amount of mobile devices made them responsible for a global internet traffic which exceeded 11.51 EiB/month in 2017, with a forecast of reaching 77.49 EiB/month in 2022 [2]. Also, the fast popularization of streaming video services, like Youtube and Netflix, allied to the growing demand for higher resolutions and frame rates, lead the industry and academia to pursuit the development of more modern video coding standards, capable of greater compression ratios. The current state-of-the-art video coding standard is the High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) [3], conceived to replace the market-dominant H.264/AVC (Advanced Video Coding). HEVC improved the compression ratios about 40% in average, when compared with H.264, keeping a similar objective video quality [4].

However, the HEVC, as well as other modern video coding standards, presents great computational effort when compared with previous standards, required due to the implementation of new tools and/or the improvement of existing ones. Depending on encoding configurations (e.g., like resolution and frame rate), HEVC can be up to 500% more complex than H.264 [5]. For instance, among several encoding steps, the Residual Coding Loop (RCL) is one of the most time-consuming within HEVC, executed several times during the encoding process and responsible for up to 18% of total encoding time [6]. Note that even though these complexity constraints being critical since most of times such a process happens at devices with limited resources availability (e.g. handheld), real-time constraints also arise as a challenge in the context of video coding. Although most often video applications present soft real-time constraints, in specific video applications, such as in robotic surgeries and coupling of satellites, these constraints are harder and a performance analysis aiming the fulfilment of the deadlines is mandatory. E.g., a full high-definition (FHD) (1920x1080 pixels) video requires a minimum frame rate of 30 fps to give a continuous motion sensation, i.e., each frame can spend a maximum time of 33 ms to be processed, otherwise, the deadlines will be missed.

In fact, video coding is seen as a complex and sophisticated workload, requiring efficient platform resources management mechanisms, hardware acceleration to deal with more complex tasks, and optimized scheduling of such tasks, as a way to optimize performance and meet deadlines. To address such constraints, many approaches consider the mapping of applications onto Systems-on-Chip (SoCs), with multiple processing units, interconnected with Networks-on-Chip (NoCs), which can interconnect several processing cores by an onchip packet-switching network, allowing data to be transferred between the local memory of each core and from/to external memory [7]; compounding a complex Multiprocessor Systemon-Chip (MPSoC), capable of reducing the computational time and meeting the time constraints [8].

Nevertheless, the mapping of an application, described by parameterized task graphs, onto a given NoC, is seen as a key research problem. Indeed, the general NoC's cores mapping problem is NP-hard and its solutions are only allowed based on efficient heuristics [9] [10]. Furthermore, the performance of the NoC interconnections also arises as a critical issue regarding time constraints. In [11] it is presented an algorithm aiming to find the NoC minimum operation frequency in a given configuration which leads the system to be schedulable. Note that the choice of the best NoC configuration/application mapping, with a NoC schedulability evaluation, is not a trivial issue. Solutions found through simulation are widely used by industry and academia to address specific scenarios. However, this approach presents two main limitations: the possibility of an execution time prohibitively large; and the finite number of possible tested scenarios, since only specific ones are simulated [7]. Even though the simulation analysis could be used in specific situations, analytical methods can be used to deal with its mentioned problems, providing a schedulability evaluation of a NoC-based multicore embedded system, verifying whether or not the system can fulfill all the timing constraints, improving the design space exploration.

In this work, we propose a design space exploration of the HEVC RCL application mapped onto NoC-based multicore embedded platforms. The application workload is modeled based in Sporadic Task-Chain, mapped onto different NoC configurations, with processing elements (PEs) based on CPUs and specific developed RCL hardware accelerators. The case study considers the encoding of an FHD frame (1920x1080 pixels) in the typical and upper-bound workload case scenarios, when dealing with CPUs, and a 4K frame (3840x2160 pixels) only in the upper-bound workload case scenario, when dealing with hardware accelerators. We propose different task mappings and platform topologies, applying the developed Schedulability breakdown NoC Frequency Tracking algorithm (SNFT) over each scenario, showing when the tasks and flows are schedulable or not, for each case study.

div.head: II. LITERATURE BACKGROUND A. HEVC
div.p: In the HEVC [3] each frame is divided into basic structures called Coding Tree Units (CTU), which is a quadtree starting with the size of 64x64, 32x32, or 16x16 (smallest CTU size) in the root. The leaf nodes of a CTU-rooted are called Coding Units (CUs), always-squared shaped blocks presenting the basic information about the blocks being coded, capable of assuming a minimum size of 8x8. See in Fig. 1a a frame split in CTUs and in Fig. 1b a CTU recursively divided into CUs.

The CUs can be divided into Prediction Units (PUs), during the prediction steps, which contain information about prediction modes (intra or inter), and into Transform Units (TUs), during the RCL and after the calculation of the residues (see Fig. 1: Partitioning of (a) a frame into CTUs, (b) a CTU into CUs, and (c) a CU into TUs (adapted from [12]). in Fig. 1c the example of a residual quadtree (RQT) structure starting with a 32x32 root). Each TU contains information about the transformed and quantized blocks, always squared varying from 32x32 down to 4x4 sizes. Each coding mode (intra or inter), as well as the best partitioning, is determined in HEVC by a Mode Decision (MD) unit, based on the RD (Rate Distortion) cost, which is a trade-off between distortion (objective video quality) and bit-rate, thus, the encoder must test an exhaustive amount of encoding possibilities to make the best decision.

The HEVC encoder follows a hybrid coding model, based on the encoding of residues (the difference between the original and the predicted frame) and composed of the prediction steps (intra and inter), the transform (T) and quantization (Q) steps, and the entropy coding. In order to guarantee the same references at encoder and decoder sides, decoder steps are present into the encoder, like the inverse transform (IT) and inverse quantization (IQ). The set of steps T, Q, IQ, and IT, is called Residual Coding Loop (RCL).

During the residual coding loop, the direct transform is applied to the residues (typically a Discrete Cosine Transform -DCT), converting the information from space to frequency domain. Direct quantization reduces the magnitude of the transformed residuals, removing less important information regarding the human visual system, leading most of the quantized transformed equals to zero, which improves the entropy coding efficiency. The inverse quantization and inverse transform are used to perform the inverse operations in order to reconstruct the block, used as a reference in the encoder and decoder sides. The RCL must be executed several times during the encoding of a single frame and has been being the main goal of several works in the literature due to its complexity.

div.head: B. Performance Analysis for NoCs
div.p: Networks-on-chip (NoCs) are common architectural templates for processors with several cores. In Fig. 2 we show a Fig. 2: Example of a mesh 2D NoC 3x3 architecture with a priority-driven VCs router detailing (adapted from [10]). simplified representation of a simple 3x3 NoC architecture. All the nodes are interconnected, and each one has a processing element PE, which can be, e.g., a CPU, a GPU, a hardware accelerator, and so on, linked to a local cache, which stores local information, and a router r, which routes the data packets towards the destinations (it can be another core, the off-chip memory, etc.) [7]. The communication between the processing elements and the router is made by two unidirectional links (one from PE to r and other from r to PE). In this work, we have applied the widely used 2D-mesh topology [7] [13] [14], considering wormhole NoCs with priority-preemptive arbitration, widely studied in the literature due to their ability to provide hard real-time guarantees [10] [14].

Considering a wormhole switching network, the data are encapsulated into a packet format, further divided into a number of fixed size flits (data words) [10]. The router is based on priority-preemptive virtual channels (VCs) as a way to guarantee more predictability. Each packet has a different priority assigned, allowing packets with higher priority preempt the ones with lower priorities. See in Fig. 2 that in each input port there is a FIFO buffer storing the incoming flits of packets arriving through different VCs. The routing and flow controller decides the correct output port for each packet, according to its destination. A credit-based approach based on [15] was applied, ensuring the forwarding of the data only when there is enough space in the next router's VC.

As a way to determine if application's tasks being executed and communicating over a specific NoC can fulfill the required timing constraints, it is necessary the performing of a schedulability analysis. A system is schedulable iff all its tasks and communicating flows meet the deadlines. In this paper, we have applied the end-to-end schedulability analysis presented in [7], which ensures all tasks executing over a processing element and their respective packets flow over a NoC will meet their deadlines even in the worst-case scenario. For the analysis of packet flows, we incorporated the improvements from [14], which consider the impact of finite buffers, flow control backpressure, and multi-point progressive blocking in priority-preemptive NoCs. For a comprehensive review on NoC performance analysis, see what is stated in [16].

div.head: III. APPLICATION WORKLOAD MODELING
div.p: A co-design flow of embedded systems, which consists of a set of steps starting with the specifications of requirements and ending with the hardware/software integration into silicone chips [17], is of paramount importance today. The co-design modeling phase allows designers to explore the design space, making the best architectural choices in order to meet user requirements, platform and application constraints during the development phase [8].

This work follows a modeling based on Sporadic Task Model [7], where an application is modeled as a taskset Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 ,..., τ n }, where each task τ i is a 6-tuple τ i = {C i , T i , D i , J i , P i , φ i }, which are respectively the worst-case computation time, the period (minimum inter-release time interval), the deadline, the release jitter (time between the request of a task and it starts to be processed), the priority, and a message, defined as a 3-tuple φ i = {τ d , Z i , K i }, representing the destination task, the message's size, and the maximum release jitter (total time the packet takes to reach the destination, including preemption and interference). A sporadic task-chain X = {τ 1 , τ 2 ,..., τ x } is an ordered subset of Γ, where a task sends a message to a subsequent task in X. In this case, all tasks within X have the same period and deadline. The final task of every task-chain must be the empty set Ø.

See in Fig. 3 a simplified block diagram of the HEVC encoder and the RCL modeled as a sporadic task-chain model. Each step of the RCL is considered as a task: direct transform (T), direct quantization (Q), inverse quantization (IQ), and inverse transform (IT). In addition, the first and last tasks of the chain are memory-related tasks: MI (Memory Input) and MO (Memory Output), respectively. The first one represents the modeling of a block being read from off-chip memory until reaches T. The final task is an empty set, treated as a sink (i.e., computation time equals to zero), where the necessary information is stored for the forward steps of the encoder. The payload, given in flits, are packets containing information about the data being processed, varying the size according to the TU size (4x4, 8x8, 16x16 or 32x32), NoC flit size (depends on NoC topology), bit word size, and adopted subsampling (relation between number of luminance and chrominance samples, in this work we have adopted the widely used 4:2:0).

As a way to simplify the modeling, we have made some assumptions. We considered that all blocks of a single frame can be independently processed, allowing the exploration of maximum parallelism. In order to do that, we must consider only the processing of inter-predicted blocks in the modeled RCL, since intra-predicted blocks have strong data dependency, which narrows the full parallelism exploration. Since the majority of blocks in a real encoding are inter-predicted such assumption does not incur in lack of importance of the proposed evaluation. Moreover, we have also considered that the inter-prediction is giving to RCL always the final decision in terms of prediction modes and CU size, i.e., only the evaluation of the best TU is carried out (see that in this case we are not caring about which kind of PU decision was made, we just need to know what was the selected CU sizes, which will be the roots of the RQTs in the RCL).

To model the HEVC RCL running onto a CPU, we have first analyzed the computation time of each RCL step in HEVC. We encoded 64 frames of five video sequences (BasketballDrive, BQTerrace, Cactus, Kimono, and ParkScene) from class B (1920x1080 pixels), considering four Quantization Parameters (QPs -22, 27, 32, and 37), according to the HEVC Common Test Conditions (CTCs) [18], using the reference software HM 16.18 (HEVC Test Model) [19], running isolated into an i7 core with a fixed frequency of 3.0 GHz. The computation times of RCL tasks were obtained for each TU size (4x4, 8x8, 16x16, and 32x32) and are presented in Table I. Note that we found the average computation time, obtaining a Gaussian distribution with the measured times. The computation times applied in the modeling (showed in Table I in nanoseconds) were the upper quartiles of the distribution since we want to model worst-case scenarios. In Table I we also show the payload for each TU size, considering a packet header of two flits. Furthermore, the period of the tasks into a chain is the same and equal to the inverse of frame rate (e.g., we considered 30 fps in this work, thus the period is 33 ms). The deadline for all tasks in the chain is equal to the period.

The modeling of the RCL hardware accelerator was based in works [20], [21], and [22]. The hardware was synthesized considering a target frequency of 250 MHz and a 20% input swtiching activity, using a 45 nm Nangate standard cell library [23] with the Cadence RTL Compiler tool [24]. We considered a design wrapping all RCL steps into a single design, supporting the processing of any TU size. The accelerator (acc.) computation times (in nanoseconds) are also present in Table I. Note that we present for the accelerator the worst case computation times for all TU sizes, i.e., considering a RQT with a maximum size for a given TU. These computation times do not consider the time spent to access the data from memory, which must be taken into account according to the values presented by MI, also showed in Table I, when developing the RCL modeling.

It can be noticed that the computation times when using hardware acceleration are much faster, as was expected, enhancing the RCL performance. On the other hand, such processing elements are limited to perform only RCL tasks, being idle whilst other system activities are being processed.

div.head: IV. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: The task-chains were conceived in a modular way, as was explained in the previous section. The generic task-chain for a TU NxN is presented in Fig. 4a. Since all tasks of a chain must be mapped into the same processing element, we simplified the chain, representing the set T, Q, IQ, and IT as a single task considering their computation times, also presented in Fig. 4a. We follow a cluster-based approach, presented in Fig. 4b, to instantiate any number of task-chains as wished. To perform the RCL of a 4x4 TU a simple task-chain is necessary, called Cluster 4x4. To analyze an 8x8 TU is necessary a task-chain for the 8x8 TU plus four task-chains to 4x4 TUs (which compound the 8x8). This structure is called Cluster 8x8. When analyzing a 16x16 TU, a task-chain for 16x16 is necessary, besides four Cluster 8x8 (which already contain resources to evaluate the 4x4 TUs). Such a structure is called Cluster 16x16. Finally, to perform the evaluation of a 32x32 TU, Cluster 32x32 is built by using a sporadic task-chain for 32x32 TU, in addition to four Cluster 16x16. As explained before, 64x64 TUs are not allowed, but the CUs can assume such size. In this case, the block must be split into four 32x32 TUs, requiring four Cluster 32x32. See that in order to cover all possibilities of TU splitting (starting from a given CU size), the divisions were also considered to the maximum limit, always going to the lowest level of the RQT (leaves 4x4). See in Fig. 4c the number of TUs within a split 64x64 CU.

The performance evaluation was based on two main case studies: an upper-bound workload model, for Full High-Definition (FHD) and 4K resolutions, 1920x1080 and 3840x2160 pixels, respectively, and a typical workload model for FHD resolution. The upper-bound workload model considers a single FHD and 4K frames, equally divided into CTUs 64x64. Such a pessimist scenario consists of the assumption that the inter-prediction selected only 64x64 CUs. These CUs must be partitioned into 32x32 TUs and the RQT can reach the smallest value of 4x4 TUs, resulting in the processing of 506 64x64 blocks, for FHD, and 2024 64x64 blocks, for 4K, recursively divided until 4x4 TU sizes. Note that, regarding processing effort, no other situation is worse than this one. A schedulability test for this workload, ensuring the meeting of timing constraints, resulting in a schedulable system, automatically means that any other workload scenario will be also schedulable. However, such a pessimist scenario is not real, in a practical way would never happen.

A typical workload scenario, considering an FHD frame, must take into account the occurrence of skips and the average CU size selection. A skip occurs when the predicted block is equal to the original. In this case, the generated residue will be equal to zero. Therefore, the RCL can be skipped since the resulting transformed and quantized coefficients will also be equal to zero. This way, all effort demanded to process the RCL of this block will be avoided. The average skip occurrence in FHD videos is about 73.5% [25]. The percentual of selection of each CU in HEVC was obtained using results presented in [26] combined to in-house experiments using the reference software: 64x64 (5.86%), 32x32 (19.49%), 16x16 (35.21%), and 8x8 (39.44%). In terms of processing effort, the combining of skip occurrence and the percentual of CU selection results in a scenario (in terms of required processing), equivalent to process 136 64x64 blocks, each one split into four TUs 32x32, recursively divided until 4x4 TU sizes.

The task mapping step is a critical part of the development. This process defines where each task of the application is mapped onto which processing core, i.e., where each task is executed. A baseline approach, which is simple but not particularly efficient, is a random mapping, where each task is mapped to an arbitrary core, without regard to which core the other tasks of their chain have been mapped to. The obvious consequence is the increase of interference among data flows, as chained tasks will be less likely to communicate over local memory and more likely to send packets over the NoC.

A more efficient mapping approach could try to map all tasks from a chain onto the same processing core. This would not apply to memory-related tasks in a chain, as those must be mapped to cores with capabilities to access to off-chip memory through DMA (Direct Memory Access). Based on that principle, we have developed four approaches to map the workload onto NoCs, presented in Fig. 5. In Fig. 5a it is presented the Mapping Heuristic 0 (MH0) onto common CPUs, in Fig. 5b it is presented the Mapping Heuristic 1 (MH1) onto common CPUs, in Fig. 5c it is presented the Mapping Heuristic 0 (MH0) onto hardware accelerators, and in Fig. 5d it is presented the Mapping Heuristic 1 (MH1) onto hardware accelerators. MH0 consists of mapping all memoryrelated tasks in PE0, whose router is connected to the DMA. In this approach, there is an intensive traffic flow from the other processing elements towards PE0. On the other hand, MH1 tries to decrease the data flow intensity, strategically allocating DMAs in all NoC corners. In such mapping, the traffic flows are kept into smaller quadrants from the NoC, flowing from the other processing elements to the corners. For MH1 onto NoCs 2x2 and 3x3 are considered only two DMAs, in opposite corners (routers 0 and 3, 0 and 8, respectively).
Schedulability analysis for the proposed workload scenarios, combining different NoC configurations and mapping approaches were performed and presented in Section VI.

div.head: V. SCHEDULABILITY BREAKDOWN NOC FREQUENCY TRACKING ALGORITHM
div.p: A given application mapped onto a NoC can be fully schedulable or not depending on the NoC frequency. For the same configuration, only changing the NoC frequency, a previously unschedulable system can become schedulable. In order to find out the schedulability breakdown frequency, i.e., the minimum frequency that makes the system fully schedulable, we developed the Schedulability breakdown NoC Frequency Tracking algorithm (SNFT) based in [11], presented in Algorithm 1.

Firstly, it is defined an initial NoC frequency f 0 . The application model is created and then the other steps happen inside a loop. An auxiliary variable test schedulability is created to control the loop. The application is first mapped onto a NoC, next the schedulability test is performed. The definition criteria for the next NoC frequency value is different only for the first iteration, being the same for the following steps, and is based on the frequency values and on the information whether the system is fully schedulable or not, according to Algorithm 1. div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
div.p: In order to perform the schedulability evaluation of the HEVC RCL modeling, two experimental setups were proposed. One proposing 18 different scenarios when using CPUs as PEs is presented in Table II. Each experiment has an identification number (Exp. ID), mapped onto NoCs 2x2, 3x3, 4x4, and 5x5. The considered workloads are the ones mentioned in Section IV (upper-bound and typical for an FHD frame). Note that upper-bound was analyzed only for 4x4 and 5x5 NoCs due to the fact that, according to the high number of tasks, there are no available PEs to map all tasks from this workload onto a NoC smaller than 4x4. The mapping strategies are two: MH0 and MH1. We also considered two types of PE distribution: a maximum PE utilization (MPEU), where we map a number of tasks near to the supported limit of the PE, i.e., a sum up of task's worst case response times near to the deadline (which can imply in sub utilization of PEs sometimes, or even PEs without mapped tasks since the total number of tasks can be smaller than the PE's availability), and an uniform PE utilization (with equal task distribution among all the processing elements of the NoC).

The other experimental setup, presented in Table III, is similar to the previous one, only changing the processing elements for hardware accelerators as well as changing the workload, with the evaluation of an upper-bound 4K frame. The platform follows the architecture stated in Section II, with homogeneous CPUs or hardware accelerators, running priority-preemptive task schedulers, 2D-mesh NoC interconnected with XY dimension routing, distributed memory, 8 virtual channels with priority-preemptive link arbitration. We have applied the SNFT for each experiment as well as the schedulability analysis. Note that the tasks are always schedulable since we have previously analyzed the capacity of each processing element. On the other hand, the flows depend on NoC resources and the path they need to cross until reaching the destination. The SNFT behavior for each experiment, presented in Fig. 6, shows the number of unschedulable flows for each experiment running at different NoC frequencies, thus verifying what NoC frequency become the system fully schedulable.

In Fig. 6a is presented the SNFT behavior for a typical workload running onto CPU-based NoC, in Fig. 6b it is presented the SNFT behavior for an upper-bound workload running onto CPU-based NoC, and Fig. 6c it is presented the SNFT behavior for an uper-bound workload running onto a hardware accelerator-based NoC. Note that the system becomes schedulable depending on the NoC frequency, which varies according to the NoC size, workload and type of mapping. See that the minimum NoC frequencies happen for experiments considering bigger NoC sizes, with MH1 mapping strategy and uniform processing elements utilization. It happens because at these experiments an uniform flow dis- tribution over the NoC is favored, decreasing the preemption and interference over the packets. In addition, note that some experiments present the same NoC frequency behavior, like 02 and 10, in Fig. 6a, 12 and 16, in Fig. 6b. It happens due to the adopted mapping strategy, which lead the task distribution over the processing elements to a similar pattern.

In Fig. 7 we present the schedulability analysis results, showing the experiment's worst case latencies as box plots, based on [7] and [14]. In Fig. 7a it is presented the packet's end-to-end worst case latencies for experiments from Table II, with a target NoC frequency of 100 MHz. See that, for these configurations, only experiments 03, 05, 07, 09, and 17 are fully schedulable. Among them, experiments from 03 to 09 consider a typical FHD frame workload. Note that the system is fully schedulable with a 3x3 NoC, connected to off-chip memory using only one DMA and with uniform task PE distribution (experiment 03). Although other configurations also being schedulable, they spend more resources, which makes experiment 03 the best configuration when mapping a typical workload. Regarding upper-bound FHD frame workload, the only configuration that is fully schedulable is experiment 17. Therefore, the system will be fully schedulable when the HEVC RCL is mapped onto a 5x5 NoC, connected with four DMAs and uniform task PE distribution. In this case, we can guarantee that the system will be always schedulable since the time constraints were met even for the worst case.

Taking into account the SNFT usage, we have also analyzed the packet's end-to-end latencies of CPU-based experiments, presented in Fig. 7b, but this time considering each experiment running at its schedulability breakdown NoC frequency. Note that experiments 12 and 16 are unschedulable even at 1.2 GHz (configured as upper boundary NoC frequency in SNFT). Regarding the other experiments, all of them presented endto-end latencies smaller than the deadline, being fully schedulable. Finally, considering the accelarator-based experiments, in Fig. 7c are present the worst case latencies from tasks, flows (packets), and end-to-end. Note that all experiments were schedulable (obviously at different NoC frequencies), but it can be noticed the greater influence of the flows into the end-to-end schedulability. The usage of hardware acceleration makes the system faster, being able to process higher resolutions using the same NoC topologies applied with common CPUs as processing elements.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Many works in the literature aim the modeling of HEVC in higher abstraction levels. In [8], besides modeling the HEVC video decoder with Synchronous Data Flow in order to solve problems of placing and scheduling the application onto an embedded platform, they consider only the decoder and apply simulation methods to analyze the system. Works [27] and [28] also propose HEVC modeling in higher levels of abstraction. In [27] is developed a synthetic workload generation of broadcast-related HEVC stream decoding in constrained systems. Work [28] proposes a dynamic and static task allocation for hard real-time video stream decoding on NoCs. Although modeling the HEVC in higher levels of abstraction, these works consider only the decoder and they do not model specific steps of the encoder, like RCL, not applying hardware acceleration as well. To the best of the author's knowledge, it is the first work in the literature proposing a design space exploration of the HEVC RCL mapped onto embedded platforms based on NoCs, considering different processing elements, and performing a schedulability evaluation to meet the real-time constraints of the application.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this work we presented a design space exploration of HEVC RCL applications mapped onto NoC-based embedded platforms. The application was modeled based on Sporadic Task Model, following a cluster-based approach. Three workloads were generated (upper-bound for FHD and 4K resolutions, and typical for FHD resolution), regarding characteristics of the HEVC encoder. Two set of experiments were built, combining workloads, NoC configurations, different processing elements, and different task mapping strategies. For each configuration, a schedulability analysis was applied in order to verify if the system meets the real-time constraints posed by the application. In addition, we have also proposed the SNFT algorithm, which finds the minimum NoC frequency that allow system fully schedulable, for a given configuration.
